zh.q: 地面一样热的时候，空气会自己绕着走吗？
zh.concl: 地面受热均匀时没有相对上升和下沉；地面冷热不均是热力环流的起因——A 地受热多，空气膨胀上升，B、C 受热少，空气收缩下沉。
points: 大气运动有垂直运动和水平运动之分：垂直运动表现为气流上升或下沉，水平运动即是风。
当地面受热均匀时，空气没有相对上升和相对下沉运动（教材图 2.11a 画的就是这个状态：四条等压面都是平的）。
一旦 A 接受热量多、B 和 C 接受热量少，A 地近地面空气膨胀上升、B 和 C 收缩下沉；参考工况温差 5 K 时近地面风速 4.6 m/s。

zh.q: 空气升上去以后，为什么分头往两边跑？
zh.concl: 受热处上空空气聚积、密度增大形成高气压，未受热处上空密度减小形成低气压；高空气流由受热处上空流向未受热处上空。
points: A 地近地面空气膨胀上升，到上空聚积，使上空空气密度增大，形成高气压。
B、C 两地空气收缩下沉，上空空气密度减小，形成低气压。
于是空气从气压高的 A 地上空向气压低的 B、C 两地上空扩散；教材图 2.11b 就是这么画的（A 上空标「高」，B、C 上空标「低」）。

zh.q: 贴地这一层，气压怎么反过来了？
zh.concl: 受热处近地面空气上升向外流出、密度减小形成低气压，未受热处因下沉气流形成高气压；同一段上下两层的气压符号相反。
points: 在近地面，A 地空气上升向外流出后，空气密度减小，形成低气压。
B、C 两地因有下沉气流，空气密度增大，形成高气压（参考工况 A 地 1012.22 hPa、B 与 C 地 1013.25 hPa）。
同一段地面上下两层的气压符号正好相反，所以等压面在 A 处近地面下凹、在高空上凸——教材图 2.11b / c 画的就是这个弯法。

zh.q: 空气走完一圈，为什么能自己接上？
zh.concl: 近地面空气由未受热处流回受热处，与上升、高空扩散、下沉一起构成闭合的热力环流；高空与近地面的水平方向相反，判据是「由高压流向低压」。
points: 近地面的空气从 B、C 两地流回 A 地，以补充 A 地上升的空气，从而形成了热力环流。
方向判据只有一句话：空气由高压区流向低压区（水平气压梯度力是形成风的直接原因）。
所以同一个环里，高空与近地面两支的水平方向必然相反（点积 = −1）。

zh.q: 温差再大一点，这个圈会怎样？
zh.concl: 温差是环流强弱的源头：温差越大，同一高度的气压差越大、气压梯度越大、风越大。
points: 温差越大，同一高度上的气压差越大：1.03 → 2.02 hPa。
气压梯度随之增大（5.1 → 10.1 hPa/100 km），近地面风也变强（4.6 → 6.5 m/s）。
这三格读数是同一条因果链上的三个环节，不是三个独立结论。

zh.q: 台湾海峡白天吹的是哪个方向的风？
zh.concl: 白天陆地增温快、海洋增温慢，陆地空气上升、海洋空气下沉，近地面风由海洋吹向陆地。
points: 白天，陆地增温快，海洋增温慢——这是海陆风的起因。
陆地上空空气上升、海洋上空下沉，近地面风由海洋吹向陆地（海风）。
教材图 2.13a 是留给学生填的空图；本课按活动第 1 题 (1)→(4) 的顺序一层层画出来，就是那道题的答案。

zh.q: 到了夜里，风为什么反过来了？
zh.concl: 夜晚陆地降温快、海洋降温慢，海洋上空上升、陆地上空下沉，近地面风由陆地吹向海洋——海陆风昼夜反向。
points: 夜晚，陆地降温快，海洋降温慢——受热的那一段换成了海洋。
四支箭头全部翻转，近地面风由陆地吹向海洋（陆风）。
数值读数与白天完全相同：昼夜改变的是「哪一段受热」，不是环流的强弱。

zh.q: 污染企业放在城边上，为什么污染物反而进了城？
zh.concl: 中心区与郊区的温差形成热岛环流：中心区上升、郊区下沉，近地面风由郊区吹向中心区，污染企业必须布局在环流范围之外。
points: 城市中心区升温更快，空气在中心区上升、在郊区下沉；高空气流由中心区流向郊区，近地面气流由郊区流向中心区。
所以污染风险较大的工业企业若放在热岛环流范围之内，污染物会随近地面气流进入城区（浓度指数 8 % → 45 %，示意）。
城市规划时一般把这类企业布局在城市热岛环流的范围之外。

zh.q: 考核：把白天的近地面风调到 5.5 m/s 以上
zh.concl: 温差是环流强弱与风向的唯一驱动：温差越大，气压差越大，风越大；昼夜只改方向。
points: 达成风速 ≥ 5.5 m/s 的通路是把温差拉到 7.5 K 以上（7.5 K 与 8 K 都行）。
道理只有一条：温差 → 气压差 → 气压梯度 → 风。
昼夜开关不改数值，所以「拨到夜晚」帮不上忙——题干要的是白天的海风。

en.q: When the ground is equally warm, does air circulate on its own?
en.concl: With even heating there is no relative rising or sinking; uneven heating is the cause of thermal circulation: A is heated more and its air expands and rises, B and C are heated less and their air contracts and sinks.
points: Atmospheric motion is either vertical or horizontal: vertical motion appears as rising or sinking air, and horizontal motion is wind.
When the ground is heated evenly, air has no relative rising or sinking (Fig. 2.11a shows exactly this state: all four isobaric surfaces are flat).

Once A receives more heat and B and C less, near-surface air at A expands and rises while air at B and C contracts and sinks; in the reference case with a 5 K difference the near-surface wind is 4.6 m/s.

en.q: Once the air has risen, why does it split toward both sides?
en.concl: Above the heated area air accumulates and density rises to form high pressure; above the unheated areas density falls to form low pressure; upper-air flow goes from above the heated area toward above the unheated areas.
points: Near-surface air at A expands and rises, accumulates aloft and raises the air density there, forming high pressure.
Air at B and C contracts and sinks, so the air density above them decreases, forming low pressure.
So air spreads from the high pressure above A toward the low pressure above B and C; Fig. 2.11b draws exactly this (high above A, low above B and C).

en.q: Why is the pressure reversed in the layer next to the ground?
en.concl: Near-surface air over the heated area rises and flows out, lowering density to form low pressure; the unheated areas form high pressure because of sinking air; the upper and lower layers of the same section have opposite pressure signs.
points: Near the surface, after the air at A rises and flows outward, the air density decreases, forming low pressure.
At B and C sinking air increases the air density, forming high pressure (reference case: A 1012.22 hPa, B and C 1013.25 hPa).

The pressure signs of the upper and lower layers over the same section are exactly opposite, so the isobaric surface dips near the surface at A and bulges aloft; Fig. 2.11b/c draws exactly this bending.

en.q: Why does the air's path join up into a full loop on its own?
en.concl: Near-surface air flows from the unheated areas back to the heated area and, together with rising, spreading aloft and sinking, forms a closed thermal circulation; the upper and near-surface flows are opposite, by the rule "from high to low pressure".
points: Near-surface air flows from B and C back to A to replace the rising air at A, forming the thermal circulation.
The direction rule is a single sentence: air flows from high pressure to low pressure (the horizontal pressure gradient force is the direct cause of wind).
So within one loop, the upper and near-surface branches must flow in opposite horizontal directions (dot product = −1).

en.q: With a larger temperature difference, what happens to the loop?
en.concl: The temperature difference is the source of circulation strength: the larger it is, the larger the pressure difference at the same altitude, the larger the pressure gradient and the stronger the wind.
points: The larger the temperature difference, the larger the pressure difference at the same altitude: 1.03 → 2.02 hPa.
The pressure gradient rises with it (5.1 → 10.1 hPa/100 km), and the near-surface wind strengthens (4.6 → 6.5 m/s).
These three readings are three links in the same causal chain, not three separate conclusions.

en.q: Which way does the wind blow across the Taiwan Strait in the daytime?
en.concl: By day the land warms faster than the ocean; air rises over land and sinks over the ocean, and the near-surface wind blows from ocean to land.
points: In the daytime the land warms faster than the ocean; this is the cause of the sea–land breeze.
Air rises over the land and sinks over the ocean, and near-surface wind blows from the ocean to the land (sea breeze).
Textbook Fig. 2.13a is a blank diagram for students to fill in; this lesson draws it layer by layer following Activity question 1 parts (1)→(4), which is the answer to that question.

en.q: Why does the wind reverse at night?
en.concl: At night the land cools faster than the ocean; air rises over the ocean and sinks over the land, and near-surface wind blows from land to ocean: the sea–land breeze reverses between day and night.
points: At night the land cools faster than the ocean, so the heated section switches to the ocean.
All four arrows reverse, and near-surface wind blows from the land to the ocean (land breeze).
The readings are exactly the same as by day: day versus night changes which section is heated, not the strength of the circulation.

en.q: The polluting plant is at the city's edge, so why do the pollutants end up in the city?
en.concl: The temperature difference between the center and the suburbs forms the heat-island circulation: the center rises, the suburbs sink, near-surface wind blows from the suburbs to the center, and polluting plants must be located outside the circulation.
points: The city center warms faster; air rises over the center and sinks over the suburbs; upper-air flow goes from the center to the suburbs, near-surface flow from the suburbs to the center.
So if a high-pollution plant is placed inside the heat-island circulation, its pollutants are carried into the city by the near-surface flow (concentration index 8 % → 45 %, schematic).
In urban planning such plants are usually placed outside the heat-island circulation.

en.q: Assessment: raise the daytime near-surface wind above 5.5 m/s
en.concl: The temperature difference is the only driver of circulation strength and wind direction: the larger it is, the larger the pressure difference and the stronger the wind; day and night only change the direction.
points: The way to reach a wind of ≥ 5.5 m/s is to raise the temperature difference above 7.5 K (7.5 K and 8 K both work).
There is only one reason: temperature difference → pressure difference → pressure gradient → wind.
The day/night switch doesn't change the values, so switching to night doesn't help; the question asks for the daytime sea breeze.
